doc.title: Alan Broadbent interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 26, 2023

title: Frank Zappa and the discoveries in Mahler
summary: Broadbent says Zappa doesn't move him, then compares finding hidden details in Mahler to hidden treasures in his son's videogames.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well where does Frank Zappa fit in there?
And the reason I brought it up is I see that you chose one of his tunes to write a chart on.

Yeah well that was back in the day, and it was a fun tune, but you know I’m struggling myself even at this age I struggle every day to do this. But who am I to say? I feel there’s a touch of dilettantism with Frank you know. But like I said, who am I?
No I’m just not moved, that’s all.
It doesn’t have that deep thing —

Maybe it does to somebody else but I don’t have enough time. I’m still trying to figure out the mysteries of the Ninth Symphony of Mahler you know, not to mention the Tenth. You know there are all these — what my son — who is 23 now — that my son with all the videogames and stuff, there are these things, what are they called — like they’re hidden treasures they’re called. They have a name for it, oh heck he’s not here. But they’re like in the game itself there are these little things that you’ll find that add points. So you might sort of miss them as you’re going by but ooh there’s one. And that’s happening to me constantly in a Mahler symphony. It’s like, oh you mean that little phrase there that I’ve been listening to for twenty years is that one that’s down there, that he’s down in the basses, oh. You know stuff that any scholar could have just pointed out to me in a half a minute, but the sense of self discovery that I have with this music is —
